newsitem.title: USA: Apple Chairman Amelio resigns, Jobs to expand role.
newsitem.headline: Apple Chairman Amelio resigns, Jobs to expand role.

text.p: Apple Computer Inc. Wednesday said Chairman and Chief Executive Gilbert Amelio resigned Tuesday night, after struggling fruitlessly for 17 months to return the company to profitability.

In a surprise statement, Apple said until a new CEO is found, Steve Jobs, the ousted Apple co-founder who returned in December to advise Amelio, will assume an expanded role, fuelling speculation he may once again lead the troubled computer maker.
In a related move, Ellen Hancock, executive vice president of technology, also plans to leave Apple. Hancock was hired by Amelio to help Apple regain its technological edge.
Her responsibilities have been reassigned to Avie Tevanian and Jon Rubinstein.
Amelio is the latest in series of top executives to leave Apple as it has suffered through years of falling sales and missed opportunities.

In 1985, John Sculley ousted Jobs in a stunning boardroom coup. Eight years later, Sculley was replaced by Michael Spindler, who remained at the helm until 1996 when he was forced to step down in favour of Amelio.

"We recognise a lot has been accomplished in the last year and a half under Gil's tenure" said Chief Financial Officer Fred Anderson. "But the fact is we're not yet on a growth path and we haven't returned the company to sustainable profitability."

Since Amelio arrived at Apple in February 1996, Apple has gone through two massive restructurings, fired thousands of employees, replaced its entire suite of senior executives and discontinued several unprofitible products. But the company has bled red ink every quarter, except for one. Its revenue is expected to shrink to about $8.5 billion in the latest fiscal year from $11.1 billion in fiscal 1995.

While Amelio had won some praise for quickly shoring up Apple's weak finances upon his arrival, customers and investors criticised him for failing to come up with a strategy that would stave off the popularity of personal computers based on Microsoft Corp. and Intel Corp. technology.
"Amelio underestimated the extent of the problems at Apple when he got there," said David Wu, analyst at investment bank ABN AMRO Chicago Corp.
Added Lou Mazzucchelli, analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison: "He needed to fill the role of a visionary leader, which he didn't fit well."

Apple said it has begun looking for a new CEO. Until one is found, Anderson will handle day-to-day operations. Jobs will help the company with product strategy, marketing and business partnership, Anderson said.
Anderson refused to comment whether Jobs is in the running to replace Amelio.
